passages.title: The promised answer creates a second complaint
passages.summary: Habakkuk asks how long he must cry for help and not be heard. He sees violence, and justice never wins. God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans. They are a fierce nation that sweeps across the earth. Their own strength is their god. Habakkuk objects that God’s eyes are too pure to look on evil. He asks why God is silent while the wicked swallow the more righteous. The enemy catches people like fish in a net.
passages.uncertainty: The complaint names no city where the prophet stands. The conquerors receive no reconstructed army route.

lds.text: The lesson invites readers to bring difficult questions to God as Habakkuk does. Why does the announced rise of Chaldeans create a second complaint?

contextNote.title: The promised answer creates a second complaint
contextNote.text: Habakkuk’s first complaint is about wrong inside Judah (verses 2–4). God’s answer is the coming of Babylon (verses 5–11). That answer creates a second complaint. Verse 13 argues from God’s own character. A pure God is using a nation worse than the one it punishes. Verses 15–17 picture people as fish and the empire worshiping its net. The book records a prophet arguing with God.

passages.title: The victimized peoples gain a voice against their captor
passages.summary: Habakkuk stands at his watch post to see what God will say. The LORD tells him to write the vision plainly on tablets. It awaits its time, and he must wait for it. The proud one is not upright, and the righteous will live by faith. The conquered nations will taunt their conqueror with five woes. He piled up what was not his and built his house on plunder. Idols are teachers of lies. The LORD is in his holy temple, and all the earth must be silent.
passages.uncertainty: The marker locates a broad regional reference. No watchtower or poetic divine route is assigned.

lds.text: The lesson connects the prophet’s watch with waiting for answers from God. Why do stones and beams testify against their owner?

contextNote.title: The victimized peoples gain a voice against their captor
contextNote.text: Verse 6 says the conquered peoples will speak these woes. They receive a voice against their captor. Verses 9–11 concern a house built with unjust gain. The builder hoped to set his nest out of harm’s reach. Verse 11 says the stones and beams themselves will accuse him. No human witness is needed. Verse 4 tells the righteous how to live while they wait.

passages.title: The song chooses joy without claiming that food has returned
passages.summary: Habakkuk prays and asks God to remember mercy in his anger. He recalls God coming from the south in glory. Mountains shook, and the sun and moon stood still. God went out to save his people and crush the wicked. Habakkuk’s body trembles as he waits for the day of trouble. The fig tree may not bud, and the fields may give no food. The flocks and herds may be gone. Yet he will rejoice in the LORD, who is his strength.
passages.uncertainty: The marker locates a broad regional reference. No watchtower or poetic divine route is assigned.

lds.text: The lesson studies rejoicing in God when material sources of security fail. Which losses remain when the speaker chooses to rejoice?

contextNote.title: The song chooses joy without claiming that food has returned
contextNote.text: Verse 17 lists six losses. Figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep, and cattle all fail. That is the whole food supply of a farming land. Verse 18 begins with “yet.” Nothing in the list is said to return. His joy is placed in God, apart from the harvest. Verse 16 shows that his body still trembles as he says it.

words.label: Sheol

words.label: Anoint
words.meaning: To pour oil on a person or thing to set it apart. Kings and priests were anointed.

words.label: Remnant
words.meaning: The part of a people that survives a disaster.
